questions.text: How many AI-powered decision systems does your organisation currently operate?
questions.rationale: The standard requires a current inventory of every AI system making or influencing consequential decisions (HU-3). Organisations routinely undercount here — the number given at the start of an audit is rarely the number found by the end of it.

options.text: None — we are evaluating AI adoption

questions.text: Does your organisation build, train or sell AI systems that other organisations use to make decisions?
questions.rationale: Division 5 (Artificial) exists for builders, whose accountability runs upstream — they are responsible for the accountability architecture their customers’ decisions rest on. Being certified as a builder does not relieve your customers of needing their own certification.

options.text: No — we only use AI internally
We build internal tools, not sold externally
Yes — we develop and sell AI systems or models to others

questions.text: Do any of your AI systems make decisions that produce legal effects (e.g. loan denial, hiring, medical diagnosis)?
questions.rationale: This is the single question that most determines your Division, and the one POPIA §71 turns on: a decision with legal or substantially similar effect, made solely by automated means, requires safeguards and an explanation.

options.text: No, purely advisory or internal use
Yes, but humans review all final outputs
Yes, some decisions are fully automated

questions.text: Do your systems process special personal information (health records, biometrics, children's data, criminal history)?
questions.rationale: Special personal information raises the stakes on disparate impact testing (EM-7) rather than changing the requirements themselves. Where it is core to the system, refusing to supply disaggregated outcome data at audit is recorded as Not Testable — which is itself a finding.

options.text: No special personal data is processed
Yes, core functionality relies on special data

questions.text: What is the primary deployment environment of your AI systems?
questions.rationale: Who is on the receiving end determines which requirements apply and how hard the evidence bar sits. A system affecting the public carries disclosure and correction duties that an internal tool does not.

options.text: Customer-facing, high stakes (e.g. credit decisions, claims)

questions.text: What volume of decisions does your AI system process monthly?
questions.rationale: Volume is what makes silence suspicious. Across material decision volume, zero overrides (HU-7) and near-zero appeal uptake (CO-7) are not evidence that nothing went wrong — they indicate a control nobody is using or nobody can find.

questions.text: Is there a documented process for humans to intervene in AI decisions?
questions.rationale: The standard separates having an override process (HU-4) from the override actually working in production (HU-5) — the second is demonstrated live at audit, because a documented process nobody has exercised is a document, not a control.

options.text: Ad-hoc intervention is possible but not documented
Formal review process for flagged cases only
Mandatory human sign-off on all critical outputs

questions.text: Who is accountable for the AI system's outcomes in your organisation?
questions.rationale: Accountability must attach to a named individual, not a role or a department (HU-1), and that person signs a declaration accepting it personally (HU-2). At audit they must be able to describe operational reality unaided — needing to check with someone else is a finding (HU-11).

options.text: Product Owner or Business Unit Head

questions.text: Do you track the rate at which humans override AI recommendations?
questions.rationale: Overrides must carry a stored reason (HU-6), and the override record is the primary evidence that oversight is real. This is the metric AIC treats as load-bearing: an untracked override rate cannot be distinguished from an override rate of zero.

options.text: Yes, formal metrics tracked and reviewed monthly

questions.text: Are decision-makers trained on the limitations and potential biases of the AI model?
questions.rationale: An override right that the operator does not know how to exercise, or does not know when to exercise, is not oversight. This bears directly on whether the Accountable Person can describe operational reality unaided at audit (HU-11).

options.text: Regular, documented training on bias and limitations

questions.text: Can an affected person appeal a decision made or influenced by the AI?
questions.rationale: The correction route must be publicly accessible (CO-1) and findable by an ordinary person rather than someone who already knows it exists (CO-2) — at audit, the assessor must locate it unaided. A named human must own the response (CO-9).

options.text: Dedicated appeal workflow with guaranteed human review

questions.text: How quickly can a human intervene to stop the AI from making further decisions?
questions.rationale: The override must be functional and demonstrable in the production system (HU-5), and the escalation path traceable end to end (HU-9). An intervention that requires an engineering ticket is not an intervention available at decision speed.

questions.text: Do you have a policy for how long AI decisions can operate without human review?
questions.rationale: The observed oversight ratio must be consistent with the Division you have declared (HU-8). Declaring Supervised while operating at Monitored review rates is the specific mismatch Pulse monitoring exists to catch between audits.

options.text: Formal policy with defined review intervals

questions.text: Do users know they are interacting with an AI system?
questions.rationale: Disclosure must occur before the interaction affects the person (TR-3) and be specific about what the AI does in this decision (TR-4). A terms-and-conditions checkbox at signup generally fails for a decision made months later.

options.text: Prominent disclosure at point of interaction

questions.text: Can you explain WHY the model reached a specific decision to an affected person?
questions.rationale: The hardest requirement in the standard sits here: the reason given must materially match the actual driver of the decision (EX-5). Divergence between the stated reason and the dominant feature is a critical finding — that is rationalisation, not explanation.

options.text: No, it is a "black box" model
Yes, full decision logic is interpretable and documented

questions.text: Is there documentation of how the AI model was trained and validated?
questions.rationale: A current model card or equivalent is required (EX-7), including identification of proxy variables (EX-6). Vendor documentation alone does not discharge this where the deploying organisation cannot say what the model actually uses.

options.text: Full internal documentation including data sources and validation

questions.text: Have you tested the AI for bias across protected characteristics (race, gender, age)?
questions.rationale: Bias testing must be recent, scoped and methodologically sound (EM-6), and the disparate impact ratio must reach at least 0.8 across tested characteristics (EM-7). Testing once during development does not survive a model that has since been retrained.

options.text: Regular bias audits with documented results

questions.text: Do you maintain records of individual AI decisions for audit purposes?
questions.rationale: Explanations must be retained and retrievable per individual decision (EX-3), and correction requests logged immutably with their outcome (CO-5). Aggregate statistics cannot answer a question about one person’s decision, which is the only question that person is asking.

options.text: Full decision audit trail with inputs and outputs

questions.text: Does your organisation have an AI governance policy or framework?
questions.rationale: Governance is what makes the named accountability (HU-1) and the system inventory (HU-3) survive staff turnover. Without it, both tend to exist in one person’s memory, which is not a control that outlives them.

options.text: Dedicated AI governance framework with defined roles

questions.text: How do you handle data privacy in your AI systems (POPIA compliance)?
questions.rationale: POPIA §71 is the binding local hook for automated decision-making, and a documented AI disclosure policy (TR-1) with a current public statement (TR-7) is the visible half of discharging it.

options.text: Basic POPIA compliance measures in place
Comprehensive privacy impact assessment for AI systems

questions.text: Do you have insurance coverage or legal protections for AI-related liability?
questions.rationale: This maps to no requirement in the standard — AIC does not assess your cover. It is asked because underwriters increasingly do, and because the answer tells you where the liability currently sits if a decision goes wrong tomorrow.

categories.name: AI Usage Context
categories.purpose: Establishes which Division your organisation would be assessed in. Divisions are modes of operation, not grades — a Supervised organisation is not worse than a Sovereign one, it is answering a different set of requirements.

categories.name: Human Oversight
categories.purpose: Tests whether a named human is genuinely accountable and can actually intervene. Weighted heaviest because every other right depends on someone being able to stop, reverse or explain a decision.

categories.name: Transparency
categories.purpose: Tests whether people know an AI is involved before it affects them, and whether the reason they are given is the reason that actually operated.

categories.name: Infrastructure & Compliance
categories.purpose: Tests whether the governance around the systems exists as structure rather than intention — policy, privacy posture, and where liability currently sits.
